name: Zero-carb carnivore

lead: The zero-carb carnivore diet allows only animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs and sometimes dairy, with no plants and no added carbohydrate. People follow it to drop fat, keep muscle and, they report, calm skin and inflammation.

The chain is high protein and fat, which keeps appetite low, so intake falls and the body gets leaner; with almost no carbohydrate the body usually runs on fat and ketones. Shawn Baker and the Petersons helped popularise it from about 2017 to 2019. Published data consist of a 2021 self-selected survey, case reports and small series.

paras: Meals are built from beef, fish, eggs and sometimes dairy, with trace carbohydrate from animal sources accepted. Followers often eat to appetite rather than counting calories, and some use it as a strict reset, then keep or loosen it. Users commonly report changes in weight and digestion within weeks.

Reported or discussed risks include no fibre, possible shortfalls of vitamin C and other micronutrients, sharply raised LDL cholesterol in some people, constipation, gout and kidney strain. The British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia classify it as a fad diet, and long-term safety has not been established.

angle.text: Followers eat only animal foods so high protein keeps appetite down, body fat drops and muscle is held, with clearer skin and less inflammation reported along the way. The support is mainly self-reported surveys and case reports.

lead: The carnivore diet, also called the zero-carb diet, is a high-protein, low-carbohydrate regimen in which adherents eat only animal products such as meat, dairy and eggs.[1] Grokipedia describes the strict zero-carb version as the baseline, with no plants and no added carbohydrates, and trace carbohydrates from animal sources generally under 5 grams a day considered acceptable.[2]

Orthopaedic surgeon Shawn Baker promoted the diet on social media from 2018, and Jordan and Mikhaila Peterson became prominent adherents.[1] Supporters rely mainly on self-reported surveys and anecdotes; Grokipedia describes controlled long-term evidence as largely missing, while professional dietetic bodies regard the diet as a fad.[1][2]

paras: Zero-carb eating excludes all plant foods and relies on fat and protein for energy, usually through ketosis.[2] Variants include stricter beef-only forms, inclusive versions with poultry, fish, eggs and low-lactose dairy, ketovore versions allowing about 10 grams of carbohydrate a day from low-carb plants, and the animal-based approach that permits fruit and honey.[1][2]

Bernard Moncriff's 1856 book promoted an exclusively animal diet, Arnaldo Cantani used animal-based diets for diabetic patients in the 1870s, and James H. Salisbury advocated lean beef and hot water in the 1880s.[1] Grokipedia cites John Rollo's 1797 diabetes treatment, reanalysed Inuit records suggesting roughly 10 percent of energy from carbohydrate, and Vilhjalmur Stefansson's medically observed meat-only year in 1928 and 1929.[2]
Baker's 2017 appearance on the Joe Rogan Experience, his 2019 book and the Petersons' public testimony drove popularity in the late 2010s.[2]

Advocates say the diet stabilises blood sugar and insulin, aids weight loss, eases autoimmune, digestive, skin and mood problems, and provides bioavailable nutrients.[2] Grokipedia notes that lipid changes are mixed, with triglycerides falling and HDL rising but LDL often rising.[2]

Wikipedia lists the lack of fibre, vitamin deficiencies from excluding fruit and vegetables, raised LDL cholesterol, constipation, higher risk of colon cancer and gout with high red-meat intake, and possible kidney impairment, and says professional bodies treat it as a fad diet.[1]

Grokipedia adds a documented scurvy case, LDL levels exceeding 500 mg/dL in some cases, kidney-stone concerns, and transient early fatigue and cramps attributed to electrolyte loss. It also describes a pilot microbiome study finding normal diversity and notes advocates who argue the LDL particles are benign, a view it says mainstream guidance disputes.[2] It also records an environmental debate, with critics citing emissions and supporters citing regenerative grazing.[2]

No controlled trials of a long-term zero-carb carnivore diet have been published according to the sources reviewed. Evidence consists of a 2021 survey of 2,029 adherents, of whom 95 percent reported overall improvement, a self-selected sample prone to bias, along with case reports and small series, such as a 2024 series of 10 patients with inflammatory bowel disease reporting clinical remission.[2]

lore.intro: Carnivore advocates present the diet as a human-optimal elimination diet.[2]

claims.claim: No plant foods are needed and plants can be harmful.
Zero-carb carnivore reverses type 2 diabetes and aids weight loss.
High LDL on carnivore is harmless.
